title: Boss: capacity and failure
summary: Reliability tickets: Pending pods and OOM kills on a real Kubernetes cluster, then an autoscaling capacity plan.

steps.title: The scene
body: Reliability tickets. The first two open their own one-node **Kubernetes 1.37** cluster with the problem happening:
read `kubectl describe`, `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` and the containers' `lastState`, then fix the
resources. The last one is capacity planning on paper, before Black Friday.

steps.title: Ticket 1: pods stuck in Pending
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). `search` has two pods that have been `Pending` since it was deployed. Find out why from the
scheduler's events, and fix the Deployment's resources (the service needs about `256Mi` of memory) so that both pods

checks.name: both search pods run
checks.cmd: kubectl rollout status deploy/search --timeout=40s >/dev/null; kubectl get deploy search -o jsonpath='{.status.readyReplicas}'

checks.name: its memory request is realistic
checks.fail: Request what the service needs (`256Mi`), not 64 GiB.

hints: `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` (or `kubectl describe pod -l app=search`) shows `FailedScheduling ... Insufficient memory`.
The pods ask for 64Gi; `kubectl describe node dojo` shows what the node can allocate.
solution: kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | grep FailedScheduling | tail -n 1
kubectl describe node dojo | grep -A6 Allocatable
steps.explain: The scheduler places a pod only on a node whose **allocatable** capacity minus other pods' **requests** covers its requests; actual usage does not matter. `Insufficient memory` in a `FailedScheduling` event is the whole diagnosis, and the fix is either a realistic request or more capacity (the cluster autoscaler reacts to exactly these Pending pods).

steps.title: Ticket 2: something keeps getting OOM-killed
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). Three workers run here, and one of them keeps restarting. Find the one that is killed for using too much
memory (its container's **last state** says so), write its Deployment's name into `~/answers/oom.txt`, then give it a
memory limit (and request) of `128Mi` so it stays up and logs `ready`.

checks.name: oom.txt names the OOM-killed worker
checks.fail: Not the right one. `kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount,LAST:.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.reason`.

checks.name: thumbnails is up with a 128Mi limit
checks.cmd: kubectl rollout status deploy/thumbnails --timeout=40s >/dev/null; sleep 3; kubectl get deploy thumbnails -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.limits.memory}'; echo; kubectl logs $(kubectl get pods -l app=thumbnails -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | select(.metadata.deletionTimestamp == null)] | sort_by(.metadata.creationTimestamp) | last | .metadata.name') --tail=1
checks.fail: `thumbnails` should run with a `128Mi` limit and log `ready`.

hints: `kubectl get pods` shows which one restarts; `kubectl describe pod NAME` shows `Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137`.
steps.explain: An OOM kill shows up as a restart with `lastState.terminated.reason: OOMKilled` and exit code 137, while the current state already says `Running` again, which is why the RESTARTS column and `describe` are where you see it. Raising the limit is the quick fix; the lasting one is knowing the working set (from metrics) and setting the request and limit from it.

steps.title: Will the HPA's pods fit?
prompt: Combine the HPA and capacity. Write `string Plan(int current, double cpuUtil, double target, int min, int max, int podCpuM, int clusterFreeCpuM)`:
- compute desired replicas exactly as in the HPA lesson (10% tolerance, ceil, clamp)
- `extra = desired - current`; if `extra <= 0` return `"scale to D"`
- pods that fit = `clusterFreeCpuM / podCpuM` (integer division). If all extra pods fit, return `"scale to D"`; otherwise `"scale to D, N Pending"` where N is how many will not fit.
starter: string Plan(int current, double cpuUtil, double target, int min, int max, int podCpuM, int clusterFreeCpuM)
solution: string Plan(int current, double cpuUtil, double target, int min, int max, int podCpuM, int clusterFreeCpuM)
return fit >= extra ? $"scale to {desired}" : $"scale to {desired}, {extra - fit} Pending";
template: Dojo.Eq("not enough room", "scale to 10, 3 Pending", Plan(5, 120, 60, 2, 10, 500, 1200));
hints: Integer division gives how many pods fit.
steps.explain: This ticket stays a code step: it is capacity planning on paper (the HPA formula against free CPU), done before the incident, with no cluster to look at.
